caption: Figure 3: Test solve rate after finetuning a 6B model on the full GSM8K training set, when the model is allowed to make 1 guess (left) or 100 guesses (right).
description:
Section 1: Figure description
This figure consists of two line graphs, each showing the test solve rate of a 6B model after finetuning on the GSM8K training set. The left graph displays the Test@1 Solve Rate, while the right graph shows the Test@100 Solve Rate. Both graphs have epochs on the x-axis and solve rates on the y-axis.

Section 2: Figure details
Test@1 Solve Rate: The 6B model's Test@1 Solve Rate starts at 12% and increases to 22% by epoch 50. The highest point is at epoch 10 with 22%, and the lowest point is at epoch 0 with 12%.
Test@100 Solve Rate: The 6B model's Test@100 Solve Rate starts at 84% and decreases to 70% by epoch 50. The highest point is at epoch 0 with 84%, and the lowest point is at epoch 50 with 70%.

caption: Figure 4: A diagram of the verification training pipeline.
description:
## Section 1: Figure Description
This figure is a diagram illustrating the verification training pipeline for solving math word problems. It consists of three main stages: 1) Training the generator, 2) Generating and labeling 100 solutions per problem, and 3) Training the verifier. Each stage is represented by a separate block with arrows indicating the flow of data.

## Section 2: Figure Details
The figure shows three stages: 1) Training the generator uses questions and solutions to produce outputs. 2) The generator then creates 100 solutions for each problem, which are labeled. 3) The verifier is trained using the questions, solutions, and their labels. Arrows connect the blocks, showing the data flow from one stage to the next.

description:
## Figure description
This line graph compares the performance of two verifiers over epochs. The x-axis represents the number of epochs, ranging from 0.0 to 1.0. The y-axis shows the test solve rate in percentage, ranging from 5% to 40%. Two lines are plotted: one for the token-level verifier and another for the token-level verifier with joint training. The token-level verifier starts at 5% and increases to around 35% by the end of the epochs. The token-level verifier with joint training starts at a lower rate and ends at a slightly higher rate, around 38%.

Section 1:
This figure is a line graph showing the relationship between the number of completions per test problem and the test solve rate percentage. The x-axis represents the number of completions per test problem, ranging from 25 to 3200. The y-axis represents the test solve rate percentage, ranging from 34% to 42%. The graph displays a series of data points connected by a line, indicating the trend of the test solve rate as the number of completions per test problem increases.

Section 2:
The test solve rate percentage starts at 34% when the number of completions per test problem is 25. It then increases steadily, reaching a peak of 42% at around 400 completions per test problem. After this peak, the test solve rate percentage decreases gradually, reaching 38% at 1600 completions per test problem and 36% at 3200 completions per test problem.

This figure is a flowchart illustrating the calculator sampling procedure in a model designed to solve math word problems. It shows a sequence of steps where a generator produces parts of a sentence, and a calculator evaluates the mathematical expression. The process begins with the generator creating a sentence fragment, then the calculator is triggered to evaluate the expression, and finally, the generator completes the sentence with the result.

This figure is a visual representation of a joint training objective for a model that solves math word problems. It shows two objectives: Language Modeling and Verifier. The Language Modeling Objective involves a generator that takes question tokens and produces solution tokens. The Verifier Objective involves a verifier that takes question tokens and solution tokens to predict values. The figure highlights the masking of certain tokens in the question during training, which are not considered in the loss calculation.

description:
Section 1:
This figure is a table showing five math word problems generated by a fine-tuned model and scored by a verifier. The table includes the problem statement, the model's solution, the verifier's predicted score, and the actual score. The problems cover various topics such as egg omelets, onions and potatoes, beads, and arcade spending.

Section 2:
Claire makes a 3 egg omelet every morning for breakfast. How many dozens of eggs will she eat in 4 weeks? Sophia and Rose went together to the market to buy onions and potatoes. Rose bought 4 times the number of onions and potatoes Sophia bought. If Rose bought 12 onions and 4 potatoes, how many onions and potatoes in total did Sophia buy at the market? Two sisters, Elizabeth and Margareth, bought beads. Elizabeth bought 1 pack of red and 2 packs of clear beads, while Margareth bought 3 packs of blue and 4 packs of red beads. How many more beads do one sister have than the other, if each pack of beads contains 20 pieces of beads? Howard spends $8 dollars at the arcade on Monday. On Tuesday, he spends twice as much at the arcade as he did on Monday. On Wednesday, he spends 4 times as much at the arcade as he spent on Tuesday. If he originally had $100, how much money does he have left? In a jewelers store, the price of a gold ewell is 4/5 times as much as the price of a diamond ewell. The cost of a silver ewell is $400 less than the price of gold. If a diamond ewell is $2000, find the total price for all three jewels.
